summary: Recommends improving OSPF Version 2 scalability and stability in large networks by processing Hello and LSA acknowledgment packets at higher priority and using congestion avoidance procedures. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: In a large network running OSPF, many link state advertisements can change at once and the routers become too busy to keep up. This document tells routers to handle Hello packets and acknowledgments first, to slow down retransmissions when a link is congested, and to set up only a limited number of new neighbor links at a time.

questions: what is an ospf lsa storm
how to limit simultaneous ospf adjacencies
subtitle: How OSPF routers keep Hellos and acknowledgments flowing when many link state advertisements arrive at once.

tldr.problem: In a large OSPF network, many link state advertisements can change at the same time and overload the routers, which then drop packets and declare links that still work as down.
tldr.mechanism: The document recommends five steps: handle Hello and acknowledgment packets ahead of other OSPF packets, lengthen the gap between retransmissions of the same LSA, slow down new LSAs to a neighbor that is not acknowledging them, and limit how many adjacencies are brought up at once.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice, BCP 112. The unit metadata lists it as updated by RFC 9454, so read that document alongside this one.

today: RFC 4222 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 112, published in October 2005. The unit metadata lists it as updated by RFC 9454, so read that document together with this one.

sections.title: LSA Storms and Why They Hurt
sections.content:
This document concerns OSPF Version 2, the interior gateway protocol that routers inside one autonomous system use to exchange link state advertisements (LSAs). The techniques described here may also apply to OSPF Version 3, but the document says that needs further study and operational experience.

A large network running OSPF can experience the simultaneous or near-simultaneous update of a large number of LSAs. The document calls this an LSA storm. A storm can be initiated by an unscheduled failure, which may be hardware, software or procedural in nature, or by a scheduled maintenance event. It is particularly likely when the OSPF traffic engineering extension is used, because that extension can significantly increase the number of LSAs in the network.

The storm causes high CPU and memory utilization at the router, so incoming packets are delayed or dropped. Delayed acknowledgments, beyond the retransmission timer value, result in retransmissions, and delayed Hello packets, beyond the router-dead interval, result in neighbor adjacencies being declared down. The retransmissions and the additional LSA originations raise CPU and memory utilization further, which forms a positive feedback loop that in the extreme case can drive the network to an unstable state.

The default value of the retransmission timer is 5 seconds and that of the router-dead interval is 40 seconds. There has been a lot of interest in reducing OSPF convergence time, and much shorter, sub-second Hello and router-dead intervals have been proposed. In that case a Hello packet is more likely to be delayed beyond the router-dead interval during the congestion caused by an LSA storm.
sections.plainLanguage: An LSA is the unit of information that OSPF routers send to each other about the network. When many LSAs change at the same time, routers run out of processing capacity and declare links that still work as down. The five steps in this document break that loop.

sections.title: Prioritizing Hellos and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
Recommendation 1 splits OSPF packets into two classes by examining the OSPF packet header. The high priority class holds Hello packets and Link State Acknowledgment packets, and the low priority class holds all other packets. A router should try to process a high priority packet ahead of a low priority one, both while receiving a packet from a neighbor and while transmitting a packet to a neighbor.

Prioritized processing at the transmitter can cause OSPF packets from a neighbor to be received out of sequence. When Cryptographic Authentication (AuType = 2) is used, successive valid OSPF packets received from a neighbor need to have a non-decreasing cryptographic sequence number. To comply with that requirement, the document recommends that prioritized processing not be done at the transmitter in that case, so that packets do not arrive at the receiver out of sequence. It is still useful to prioritize at the receiver, after security processing and the sequence number check are complete. Without cryptographic authentication, prioritization can be implemented at both the transmitter and the receiver.

Recommendation 2 is the fallback for routers that cannot implement Recommendation 1. Such a router resets the inactivity timer for an adjacency whenever any OSPF unicast packet, or any OSPF packet sent to AllSPFRouters over a point-to-point link, is received over that adjacency, instead of resetting it only on receipt of the Hello packet. The adjacency is then declared down only if no such packet arrives over it for a period equal to or exceeding the router-dead interval. The document does not recommend combining this with Recommendation 1, because stale packets waiting in the low priority queue could keep resetting the timer and delay the discovery that an adjacency is down.
sections.plainLanguage: Each OSPF packet goes into one of two classes: Hello packets and acknowledgments are high priority, and everything else is low priority. The router handles high priority packets first. With cryptographic authentication the ordering is only done at the receiving router, because reordering at the sender would break the sequence numbers the receiver checks.

sections.title: Backing Off Retransmissions and Slowing Delivery
sections.content:
Recommendation 3 uses an exponential backoff algorithm to set the LSA retransmission interval, RxmtInterval. Let R(i) be the interval used during the i-th retransmission of an LSA. Then R(1) = Rmin and R(i+1) = Min(K*R(i), Rmax) for i at least 1, where K, Rmin and Rmax are constants and Min returns the smaller of its two arguments. Example values are 2, 5 and 40 seconds. The example value for Rmin, the initial retransmission interval, is the same as the sample value of RxmtInterval in RFC 2328.

The reason is that repeated retransmission of LSAs is a major source of sustained congestion during a control message congestion event. Backing off reduces the rate of retransmissions while the network is congested, which helps the network get out of the congested state.

Recommendation 4 covers the case where the router itself is congested, which its neighbors cannot be told about explicitly. They can detect it implicitly from the number of unacknowledged LSAs sent to that router. Let U(t) be the number of unacknowledged LSAs to a neighbor at time t, G(t) the gap between sending successive LSAs to that neighbor, H a high-water mark and L a low-water mark. When U(t+T) is above H, the gap grows by a factor F up to Gmax; when it is between H and L the gap stays as it is; when it falls below L the gap shrinks by a factor F down to Gmin. The existing gap is only reconsidered after a time T has passed. The algorithm is applied independently to each neighbor, and only for unicast LSAs sent to a neighbor or LSAs sent to AllSPFRouters over a point-to-point link.

The two recommendations differ in what they slow down. Recommendation 3 progressively slows successive retransmissions of the same LSA, while Recommendation 4 progressively slows all LSAs, new or retransmitted, to a congested neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: When a link is congested the router slows down instead of repeating itself. It waits longer before each retransmission of the same advertisement, and it leaves a longer gap between advertisements to a neighbor that is not acknowledging them. Both rates recover gradually once acknowledgments arrive again.

sections.title: Throttling New Adjacencies
sections.content:
Recommendation 5 covers a router that tries to bring up a large number of adjacencies to its neighbors simultaneously. Database synchronization and LSA flooding for all of them can cause severe congestion. The document recommends that no more than n adjacencies be brought up simultaneously, and that newer adjacencies may be brought up once a subset has been brought up successfully, as long as the number being brought up at the same time does not exceed n.

The value of n would depend on the router's processing power, the total bandwidth available for control plane traffic and the propagation delay, and it should be configurable. For the order in which adjacencies are formed, the document recommends a First Come First Served policy based on the order in which the request for adjacency formation arrives. Requests may be from neighbors or self-generated, and among self-generated requests a priority list may be used. Once an adjacency formation process starts it is not to be preempted, except for unusual circumstances such as errors or time-outs.

Where the recommendations refer to point-to-point links, those references should also include cases where a broadcast network is treated as a point-to-point connection from the standpoint of IP routing.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that sets up many neighbor links at once spends its capacity on database synchronization for all of them. The limit on how many run at the same time keeps the rest of the router working. Requests are handled in the order they arrive.

sections.title: Appendix A: Causes and Impact of LSA Storms
sections.content:
Appendix A lists what can start an LSA storm: one or more link failures due to fiber cuts; one or more router failures, for example a software crash or a power outage affecting many routers in one office complex; link or router flapping; taking down and later bringing back many routers during a software or hardware upgrade; near synchronization of the periodic 1800-second LSA refreshes of a subset of LSAs; a refresh of all LSAs in the system during a change in software version; injecting a large number of external routes into OSPF due to a procedural error; and router ID changes that cause a large number of LSA re-originations, possibly with LSA purges as well.

More LSAs can follow the first ones. In an MPLS network, traffic engineering LSAs can be originated at other links because reserved bandwidth has changed, which happens when label switched paths that went down during the failure are rerouted. When the link recovers, additional router LSAs and traffic engineering LSAs are triggered.

The appendix defines the LSA storm size as the number of LSAs in the original storm, not counting the additional LSAs that result from the feedback loop. It notes that outage events have been reported in IP and ATM networks using link state protocols such as OSPF, IS-IS and PNNI, and that large scale flooding of LSAs was partly or fully responsible for network instability and outage in many of them. A simulation study reported in an AT&T technical report found a storm size threshold above which the network may show unstable behavior, and showed that the storm size causing instability may be substantially increased by prioritized treatment of Hello and LSA acknowledgment packets and by exponential backoff for the retransmission interval. Where Hello packets cannot be prioritized, resetting the inactivity timer on receiving any valid OSPF packet provides the same benefit. With Hello packets prioritized, links are not declared down due to missed Hellos even when the network operates above the stability threshold, so the data plane stays up while the control plane is congested.

The appendix also weighs the alternative of dividing a large network hierarchically into multiple areas so that flooding stays local. It says that approach increases network management and design complexity, may result in less optimal routing between areas, and does not help with Autonomous System External LSAs, which are flooded throughout the autonomous system, or with the summary LSAs that must be flooded across area boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: A storm starts when many advertisements change at once, for example after a fiber cut, a router failure, an upgrade, or a software error that injects many routes. Each delay and retransmission then causes more traffic. A simulation reported here found that prioritizing the key packets raises the storm size a network can survive.

sections.title: Appendix B: Variables and Example Values
sections.content:
Appendix B lists every variable used in the recommendations, with an example value. For Recommendation 3, the multiplicative constant K is 2, the minimum allowed value of RxmtInterval Rmin is 5 seconds and the maximum Rmax is 40 seconds. For Recommendation 4, the factor F is 2, the high-water mark H is 20 unacknowledged LSAs, the low-water mark L is 10, the minimum time before the existing gap is reconsidered T is 1 second, the minimum allowed gap Gmin is 20 milliseconds and the maximum allowed gap Gmax is 1 second. The limit n on the number of adjacencies brought up simultaneously has no example value.

The appendix presents these as example values rather than required settings, so a network can choose values that match its own routers and links.
sections.plainLanguage: Each variable in the steps has an example value, such as a 5-second starting retransmission interval and a 40-second maximum. The examples are not required settings. Each network chooses values that match its own routers and links.

sections.title: Appendix C: Other Suggestions
sections.content:
Appendix C offers three further ideas. The first is explicit marking: instead of examining the OSPF packet header to classify a packet, use different TOS or Precedence field settings for the two priority classes. RFC 2328 recommends setting the TOS field to 0 and the Precedence field to 6 for all OSPF packets. The document suggests keeping that setting for low priority packets and using a different setting for high priority packets, and gives two examples: TOS field 4 with Precedence field 6, or TOS field 0 with Precedence field 7. It notes that the TOS and Precedence bits have been redefined by Diffserv in RFC 2474, and that the different settings only need to be agreed among the systems on the link.

The second idea is three priority classes instead of two: high, medium and low. One candidate for the medium class is a Database Description packet from a slave used as an acknowledgment. The other is an LSA carrying intra-area topology change information, which may trigger SPF calculation and rerouting of label switched paths, so fast processing of it may improve OSPF and Label Distribution Protocol convergence times; an implementer may decide not to do this if the cost of identifying and separately queueing the LSA is high. As in Recommendation 1, when Cryptographic Authentication (AuType = 2) is used, prioritized treatment is provided only at the receiver and after security processing.

The third idea is processing a large number of LSA purges ahead of LSA originations. The document does not recommend out-of-order LSA processing, because detecting the LSA type ahead of queueing is computationally expensive, because out-of-order processing may cause subtle bugs, and because a router ID change is a relatively rare event. It does suggest that a router with a changing ID may flush the old LSAs gradually without causing a storm.
sections.plainLanguage: Three optional additions are described. A router can mark priority packets in the IP header instead of reading the OSPF header, it can add a third, medium priority class, and it could process deletions before new advertisements, though the document advises against that last one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states that this memo does not create any new security issues for the OSPF protocol.

The one security-related point inside the recommendations concerns Cryptographic Authentication. Prioritized processing at the transmitter is avoided, so that packets do not arrive at the receiver out of sequence and do not violate the non-decreasing cryptographic sequence number requirement of AuType = 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The document states that it adds no new security issues to OSPF. One rule protects the cryptographic authentication: a sending router must not reorder packets, because the receiver checks that their sequence numbers do not go backwards.

viz.caption: THE FIVE RECOMMENDATIONS IN THIS DOCUMENT

items.title: Priority classes
items.text: Handle Hello and Link State Acknowledgment packets ahead of all other OSPF packets.

items.title: Inactivity timer
items.text: Reset the adjacency timer on any OSPF packet received on it, not only on a Hello.

items.title: Retransmission backoff
items.text: Wait longer before each retransmission of the same LSA, up to a fixed maximum.

items.title: Sending gap
items.text: Leave a longer gap between LSAs to a neighbor that is not acknowledging them.

items.title: Adjacency limit
items.text: Bring up no more than n adjacencies at the same time.

viz.caption: THE TWO FORMULAS PRINTED IN RFC 4222, RECOMMENDATIONS 3 AND 4

data.title: Backoff formulas
data.code:
R(1) = Rmin
R(i+1) = Min(K*R(i), Rmax)   for i >= 1

G(t+T) = Min(F*G(t), Gmax)   if U(t+T) > H
G(t+T) = G(t)                if H >= U(t+T) >= L
G(t+T) = Max(G(t)/F, Gmin)   if U(t+T) < L
